summary: A status report on parameters, meaning numbers and keywords, used in protocols in the Internet community. It replaces RFC 1010, is historic, was updated by RFC 1349, and was replaced by RFC 1340.

eli5.summary: It is a phone book of numbers and names that protocols agree to share. This is one edition from 1990.

questions: where were protocol numbers listed in 1990
what are the arp operation codes
subtitle: The March 1990 edition of the Internet's master list of protocol numbers, ports, addresses and names.

tldr.problem: Protocols need numbers and keywords that all implementations agree on, such as IP protocol numbers, ports, multicast addresses and ARP codes. A shared, current list keeps assignments from colliding.
tldr.mechanism: This memo is a status report that collects the assigned values from many series in one document, now with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) named as the place to ask for new numbers. It adds sections that RFC 990 lacked, such as IP type-of-service values, a default TTL, multicast addresses and BOOTP parameters.
tldr.outcome: It is a snapshot of 1990, not a protocol. It is now Historic: RFC 1340 replaced it, and RFC 1349 updated it.

today: RFC 1060 is Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 1340 and updated by RFC 1349, so it is a 1990 snapshot, not a current registry.

sections.title: What the Memo Is
sections.content:
RFC 1060 is a status report on the parameters (numbers and keywords) used in protocols in the Internet community. It documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers, will be updated periodically, and points readers to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) for current information and for new assignments.

It obsoletes RFC 1010, RFC 990 and a long list of earlier RFCs and IENs. Like its predecessor, it uses bracketed references at the margin: a number cites a document and letters cite the responsible person.

It uses the usual notation: numbers in decimal, data pictured in big-endian order, and the bit labelled 0 as the most significant bit.
sections.eli5: A central office kept the list, and anyone who needed a new number asked that office.

sections.title: Special and Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
The memo says there are five classes of IP addresses, A through E. Class D and E are reserved for experimental use, and a gateway not taking part in the experiments must ignore all datagrams with a class D or class E destination address.

It then lists special cases, written as {network, host}. For example, {0, 0} is this host on this network and can only be a source address. {-1, -1} is a limited broadcast, can only be a destination, and must never be forwarded outside the (sub-)net of the source. {127, any} is the internal host loopback address and should never appear outside a host.

A multicast section lists addresses such as 224.0.0.1 (all hosts on this subnet) and 224.0.0.5 (OSPFIGP all routers). On Ethernet or IEEE 802 networks, the 23 low-order bits of the IP multicast address go in the low-order 23 bits of the multicast address.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are special on purpose. One means 'me', one means 'everybody here', and one means 'talk to myself and never leave this computer'.

sections.title: Version, Protocol and Port Numbers
sections.content:
The IP version field is 4 bits (version 4 is IP, version 5 is ST). The IP Protocol field is 8 bits and names the next-level protocol, for example 1 for ICMP, 6 for TCP and 17 for UDP.

Port numbers name the ends of logical connections. The contact port a server uses for unknown callers is the well-known port, such as 23 for Telnet, 25 for SMTP, 53 for the domain name server and 67 and 68 for the BOOTP server and client. The same assignments are used with UDP and ISO-TP4 where possible. A separate list covers Unix services: by convention, ports in the range 256 to 1024 are used for 'Unix Standard' services.

Other sections give the default IP time to live and the DNS CLASS values.
sections.eli5: Every service waits at a numbered door on the computer. This list says which door belongs to which service.

sections.title: Service, Management and Link-Layer Parameters
sections.content:
The memo introduces IP type-of-service (TOS) recommendations. There are three binary attributes: low delay, high throughput and high reliability. The recommended values have at most one bit on, since the attributes cannot all be optimized at once. Telnet and FTP control use low delay, FTP data uses high throughput, and SNMP uses high reliability. The recommended default TTL for IP is 32.

BOOTP vendor extension tags are listed (for example tag 1 is Subnet Mask with data length 4), as are SMI network management codes under the prefix 1.3.6.1.3., ARPANET and MILNET addresses and link numbers, Ethernet type numbers and vendor address components, XNS types and X.25 numbers.

For address resolution, ARP operation codes 1 and 2 are REQUEST and REPLY, while RARP uses 3 and 4. Dynamic Reverse ARP uses 5, 6 and 7. Telnet options, machine, system, protocol and terminal type names, and a numbered list of documents and people close the memo.
sections.eli5: The rest of the book is more lists: how urgent different traffic should be, what codes ask 'who has this address?', and the names of machines and terminals.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The memo says only that security issues are not discussed in it. Because it is a list of assigned values and not a protocol, there are no mechanisms in it to secure.
sections.eli5: It is a list, not a way of talking, so it has nothing to say about keeping secrets safe.
